A novel, simple, and affordable technique for arthroscopic soft-tissue tenodesis of the long head of the biceps tendon.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The purpose of this study was to describe a novel, simple, and implant-free arthroscopic soft-tissue tenodesis technique of the long head of the biceps tendon (LHBT) to the rotator cuff using an absorbable monofilament suture and to evaluate its clinical and functional outcomes at a minimum 1-year follow-up.

METHODS: A retrospective case series of 23 patients (mean age 58.0 ± 7.8 years) who underwent arthroscopic rotator cuff repair with concomitant LHBT soft-tissue tenodesis between June 2021 and June 2023 was analyzed. Functional outcomes were assessed using Constant-Murley Score (CMS), American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score, Single Assessment Numeric Evaluation (SANE), visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, and the Long Head of Biceps (LHB) score. Supination strength was measured with a handheld dynamometer and compared with the contralateral side. Incidence of Popeye deformity and tenderness over the bicipital groove were recorded.

RESULTS: Objective Popeye deformity was observed in 13% of patients, with subjective concern reported by only 4.3%. Supination strength and LHB scores were similar to the contralateral side (means of 104.65 versus 104.64 N; LHB 93.7 versus 94.6 points). The mean CMS and ASES scores were 90.3 ± 12.4 and 89.6 ± 15.9 points, respectively. The SANE score averaged 87.4 ± 20.9, and the VAS for pain was low (1.65 ± 2.59 cm).

CONCLUSIONS: This implant-free, arthroscopic LHBT soft-tissue tenodesis technique is technically simple, cost-effective, and yields excellent clinical and functional outcomes with minimal cosmetic concerns. It represents a reliable option for patients undergoing rotator cuff repair with concurrent LHBT pathology.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV.

articles.title: ORIF of three- and four-part proximal humeral fractures: a retrospective study of long-term clinical and complication outcomes of two-plate fixation methods.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: The aim of this study was to compare clinical outcomes and complication rates during long-term follow-up (≥ 6 years) after treatment for three- and four-part proximal humeral fractures using two different types of locking plates.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: A total of 113 patients with three- and four-part proximal humeral fractures who underwent surgery between September 2012 and January 2019 were enrolled retrospectively. Data for 49 patients [ 9 males, 40 females; mean age [standard deviation] (SD ) 68.9 (5.8) years} treated with a PGR (intrauma) plate (group A) and 51 patients [10 males, 41 females; mean age (SD): 66.0 (7.5) years] treated with a PHILOS humeral plate (PHP, group B) were available at the last follow-up. The mean follow-up periods in groups A and B were 10.8 and 10.2 years, respectively, with a minimum follow-up of 6 years. At the final follow-up evaluation, functional outcomes were assessed using the Oxford Shoulder Scale (OSS), Simple Shoulder Test (SST), and Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) questionnaires. X-ray evaluation was also performed, and complications were recorded.

RESULTS: The mean OSS score in the PGR and PHP groups at follow-up was 42.9 and 39.1, respectively (p > 0.05). The SST score (PGR: 7.5 ± 2.0; PHP: 7.3 ± 4.0) and DASH score (PGR: 22.1 ± 5.5; PHP: 20.5 ± 4.0) were similar in both groups (p > 0.05). In our series, 6% of patients had complications; these included avascular necrosis of the humeral head (two cases in the PGR group and three in the PHF group) and one case of periplate fracture in the PGR group.

CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with three- and four-part proximal humeral fractures, both PGR plate and PHP treatment achieved comparable functional outcomes and demonstrated similarly low complication profiles. These results reinforce the appropriate clinical utility of either implant for fixation in the treatment of this fracture pattern.

articles.title: Incidence rates and treatment of the transcervical fracture of the neck of femur in Italy: is total hip arthroplasty an increasingly preferred approach? A population study on trends between 2001 and 2023 based on 1,120,770 hospital discharge records.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Transcervical femoral neck fractures (TFNFs) are among the most devastating fragility fractures in the elderly. TFNF are associated with excess 1-year mortality rates ranging from 15% to 30%. Treatments include conservative methods, internal fixation, and arthroplasty (partial or total hip arthroplasty). This study aims to analyze the changes in incidences of TFNF in the Italian population between 2001 and 2023 and the evolution of the choices of treatment.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Using hospital discharge record (HDR) data from 2001 to 2023, records with ICD9-CM codes for femoral neck fractures (820.0 and 820.1) among diagnoses were selected and categorized into four treatment groups: total arthroplasty, partial arthroplasty, fixation, and conservative. Time series were analyzed with stratification by sex and age.

RESULTS: The extracted data included 1,120,724 records of TFNFs, with 871,161 cases treated surgically (total or partial arthroplasty or internal fixation) and 249,563 treated conservatively; the average patient age was 79.1 years, with a higher proportion of women (72.8%). Partial hip arthroplasty was the preferred treatment overall. For younger patients, in the age classes < 45 and 45-54 years, fixation was the most chosen treatment. Over time, the use of the conservative treatment decreased from 27.5% in 2001 to 14.6% of cases in 2023. The use of partial and total hip arthroplasty increased from 40% and 13.3% in 2001 to 44.5% and 24.3% in 2023, respectively.

CONCLUSIONS: Over the past two decades, Italy experienced declining age-adjusted incidence rates of TFNF despite persistent crude numbers (approximately 50,000 cases per year) owing to demographic aging. Partial hip arthroplasty (PHA) remained the preferred treatment, while total hip arthroplasty (THA) went from being the least used to the second-most performed treatment through the 23 observed years. Level of evidence level 1, population-based study.

articles.title: Does latissimus dorsi tendon transfer provide a normal scapular rhythm and external rotation strength in posterosuperior massive irreparable rotator cuff tears? A kinematic analysis in a retrospective cohort.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Posterosuperior massive irreparable rotator cuff tears (PMIRT) are rare and disabling conditions. When conservative treatment fails, latissimus dorsi tendon transfer (LDTT) is a viable surgical option for symptom relief in carefully selected patients. However, its effectiveness in restoring glenohumeral function and its influence on scapulothoracic rhythm remain subjects of ongoing debate.

PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the clinical outcomes of LDTT and assess its impact on scapulothoracic rhythm using kinematic and electromyographic analysis.

MATERIAL AND METHODS: A total of 18 patients with PMIRT underwent LDTT. Functional scores consisted of Constant-Murley score (CMS), America Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) score, and Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) score. Electromyography (EMG) activity of the latissimus dorsi muscle was evaluated in conjunction with three-dimensional (3D) kinematic tracking system. Differences in external rotation strength were compared with and without active adduction.

RESULTS: The mean age was 55.9 years (range 40-69 years), with a mean follow-up of 20.4 months (range 6-39 months). At final follow-up, the mean CMS was 68.2 (95% CI 64.9-71.5), ASES was 76.9 (95% CI 66.1-87.6), and QuickDASH was 17.6 (95% CI 9.5-25.6). A significant difference in external rotation strength was observed with and without active adduction (p < .0005). EMG confirmed latissimus dorsi activation in all patients, with no significant differences between rotation conditions (p > .05). Kinematic analysis showed an overall normal scapulothoracic rhythm, with significant differences only in scapular tilting during elevation and external rotation with the shoulder in adduction (p = 0.044 and p = 0.023, respectively).

CONCLUSIONS: LDTT provides satisfactory clinical outcomes in patients with PMIRT, enhancing external rotation strength when the latissimus dorsi is actively recruited and contributing to near-normal scapulothoracic rhythm restoration. A structured, targeted postoperative rehabilitation protocol is essential to optimize outcomes.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Is there a need for exploration in pulseless supracondylar fractures of the humerus? A systematic review and individual patient data meta-analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Different approaches have been proposed to treat patients with pulseless supracondylar humeral fractures (SHF). We aim to analyze the current outcomes of patients who have undergone different treatment options for pulseless SHF, namely watchful waiting versus urgent surgical exploration.

METHODS: Electronic databases including PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library were explored. Our study included patients from all age groups but only included English-language articles. Single case reports and case studies with adequate description of patient population, injury, and outcomes were included. An individual patient data meta-analysis was done to evaluate key outcomes of surgical exploration versus no surgical exploration in pulseless patients with SHF.

RESULTS: Overall, the data for 1070 individual patients from a total of 48 studies were included. Patients with pulseless SHF with open fractures have a higher probability of requiring vascular intervention (p < 0.001) as they are more likely to have disrupted arteries (p = 0.050) and more likely to require vascular repairs (p < 0.001) than patients with closed fractures. Similarly, patients with pulseless SHF with pucker sign (p = 0.003) and ecchymosis (p = 0.002) were more likely to undergo surgical exploration. However, the neurological status had no relation to them undergoing surgical exploration (p = 0.382), and also does not affect complication outcomes (p = 0.326) nor the need for vascular intervention (p = 1.00). However, patients with pale pulseless SHFs were more likely to undergo surgical exploration (p < 0.001), were more likely to have disrupted arteries (p < 0.001), required more vascular intervention (p < 0.001), and had a higher likelihood of complications (p < 0.001). Notably, there is no significant difference in overall complications between those who underwent exploration of arteries and those who did not among patients with pink pulseless SHF (p = 0.230).

CONCLUSIONS: Significant predictors for arterial injury requiring intervention include a pale pulseless limb, open fracture, pucker sign, and ecchymosis; expedient surgical exploration is recommended in these scenarios. However, for patients with pink pulseless SHF, watchful waiting is a viable strategy. Our meta-analysis found no significant difference in overall complication rates between patients with pink pulseless who underwent exploration and those who did not.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level II.

REGISTRATION: The review process was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines CRD.

articles.title: Increasing complexity and plateauing outcomes in AO type C distal humerus fractures: a 50-year institutional case series.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Distal humerus fractures in adults are rare but complex injuries, particularly AO type C3 fractures, often involving comminution, instability, and osteoporotic bone. Demographic trends indicate rising incidence, especially among elderly patients, with increasing functional demands challenging modern osteosynthesis. Open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) with bicolumnar plating remains the preferred reconstructive approach, although complications remain substantial. This study aimed to evaluate trends in fracture complexity, patient demographics, and functional outcomes over five decades, focusing on the most recent cohort (2009-2018, series E) and comparing with historical cohorts (series A-D, 1969-2008).

METHODS: This retrospective analysis included five consecutive 10-year institutional cohorts (series A: n = 43; B: n = 29; C: n = 47; D: n = 58) of 233 patients with 235 supradiacondylar distal humerus fractures (AO type C1-3) treated with ORIF. Functional outcome parameters (Jupiter and Cassebaum Scores) and demographic data were available for all cohorts; additional parameters (range of motion (ROM), QuickDASH Score) were available for series D and E, Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS), Short Form (SF)-36, and strength were assessed specifically in series E (n = 56; follow-up n = 21). Cross-cohort comparisons of categorical variables used chi-square tests; continuous outcomes were summarized descriptively. Historical cohort means served as a basis for comparison, and analysis of variance (ANOVA) with Tukey Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) was applied for within-series analyses.

RESULTS: Mean patient age increased to 62.6 (range 19-89, SD ± 18.1) years in series E. The proportion of AO type C3 fractures rose significantly from 11.6% (series A) to 71.4% (series E) (p ≤ 0.05). In series E (n = 56, follow-up n = 21), ORIF with bicolumnar plating was performed in 94.6% of cases and the overall complication rate was 16.4%, with mean hospitalization time of 11.1 (range 1-40, SD ± 10.1) days, mean extension deficit of 23° (range 0-90°, SD ± 26.4°), strength loss of 25.5 N (range 0-64.7 N, SD ± 19.1 N), QuickDASH Score of 23.3 (range 0-61.4, SD ± 21.2), and mean MEPS of 83.2 (range 45-100, SD ± 17.0). Good-to-excellent results were observed in 52.6% (Jupiter) and 73.7% (Cassebaum). Subjective satisfaction remained high.

CONCLUSIONS: Over five decades, distal humerus fractures increasingly involved older patients and more complex AO type C3 patterns. While ORIF continues to provide satisfactory outcomes, persistent deficits in motion and plateauing functional scores indicate that reconstructive limits may be approached in this evolving patient population.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV; Case series, treatment study.

articles.title: Magnetic resonance imaging-based fat infiltration grading improves reparability prediction in massive rotator cuff tears.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: This study aims to investigate the extent of fat infiltration (FI) in the rotator cuff (RC) muscles in more medial slices from the Y-shaped view (Y-view) on shoulder magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and assess whether these slices provide a more accurate prediction of the repairability of massive RC tears (massive RCTs).

METHODS: The retrospective study included 57 patients with massive RCTs who successfully underwent arthroscopic surgery between 1 January 2023 and 31 December 2023. Patients were categorized into two groups: the irreparable group and the reparable group. All patients underwent shoulder MRI covering the region from the acromion to the medial border of the scapula in oblique coronal and oblique sagittal orientations. The FI stage of the RC was assessed across three different views to determine which view most effectively predicts the repairability of patients with massive RCTs.

RESULTS: The FI stage of the infraspinatus (IS) muscle across three distinct views demonstrated a significant correlation with the repairability of massive RCTs. The FI stage was more severe in the irreparable group. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis revealed that the area under the curve for the 1/2 scapula view (0.737) and the most severe view (0.745) exceeded that of the traditional Y-view (0.644). Paired-sample ROC curve analysis revealed a significant difference between the most severe view and the traditional Y-view. The number of slices from the Y-view to the 1/2 scapula view was 5.89 ± 1.2. The most severe view of the IS was defined as the slice indicating the most severe FI stage, which was observed in at least two slices (84% probability) or exclusively in a single slice (16% probability).

CONCLUSIONS: This study's conclusions are based on the following findings: (1) Applying the Goutallier classification confirmed that FI in massive RCTs can extend medially to the Y-view, with the most severe FI not confined to a standard anatomical plane; (2) The concept of the "most severe view"-a nonstandardized, non-reproducible MR plane-reflects the area of peak FI. In predicting the reparability of massive RCTs, FI assessment of the IS muscle from this view demonstrates certain advantages over the traditional Y-view; however, its predictive value remains moderate. Future research should therefore focus on developing improved imaging strategies and clarifying the precise relationship between FI progression and clinical outcomes.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level IV; case-control study.

articles.title: Mid-term clinical and functional outcomes after reverse shoulder arthroplasty with latissimus dorsi transfer.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Although reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) with concomitant latissimus dorsi transfer (LDT) has been shown to effectively treat external rotation (ER) deficits, there are limited data regarding its outcomes with modern implants and its impact on activities of daily living (ADLs) requiring ER. The purpose of this study was to assess the mid-term clinical and radiographic outcomes of rTSA with concomitant isolated LDT in patients with an ER lag sign and posterior rotator cuff deficiency.

METHODS: This retrospective cohort study with prospective follow-up included consecutive patients who underwent rTSA with concomitant isolated LDT between 2010 and 2022 with a minimum follow-up of 2 years. Primary outcomes included the resolution of ER lag sign, active ER, and the Activities of Daily Living and External Rotation (ADLER) score. Secondary outcomes included the Auto-Constant Score (CS), Subjective Shoulder Value (SSV), activities of daily living requiring internal rotation (ADLIR) score, visual analog scale (VAS) for pain, and radiographic analysis of standardized radiographs.

RESULTS: In total, 32 procedures in 32 patients were identified. Of these, 22 procedures in 22 patients (68% female, 72.9 ± 8.4 years at surgery) were available for follow-up at 4.8 ± 2.2 years postoperatively (response rate 73%). The ER lag sign resolved in 95.5% of patients, the active ER improved significantly from -13° (-20-0°) preoperatively to 10° (0-20°) postoperatively (p = 0.002). The ADLER score increased from 20 (18-21.5) to 30 (28-30, p < 0.001). The CS improved from 32 (25-52) to 71 (67-75, p < 0.001) and the SSV from 30 (28-40) to 80 (65-100, p = 0.002), and low pain levels were reported. Internal rotation (p = 1) and the ADLIR score (p = 0.56) did not improve or decrease. No revisions or complications were observed.

CONCLUSIONS: rTSA with concomitant isolated LDT resulted in favorable clinical, functional, and radiographic mid-term outcomes, with a high rate of resolved external rotation lag sign and a significant improvement in activities of daily life that require ER. This procedure should be considered a viable treatment option in patients undergoing rTSA with posterior rotator cuff deficiency and an ER lag sign.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV, retrospective case series.

articles.title: Partial versus full revision in cementless single-stage exchange for hip periprosthetic joint infection: a multicenter comparative study with 10-year survivorship analysis.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) is one of the most challenging complications following total hip arthroplasty (THA). Traditional management typically involves full revision to ensure comprehensive infection eradication. However, for patients with well-fixed implants, partial revision in a single-stage cementless approach may provide a viable alternative, potentially preserving bone stock and reducing operative time. The relative efficacy of this approach compared with full revision remains to be fully explored. This multicenter study aims to determine whether partial revision in cementless single-stage exchange surgery offers comparable infection control outcomes to full revision for select patients with well-fixed implants.

METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, multicenter cohort study involving 226 patients who underwent cementless single-stage exchange hip arthroplasty for PJI between 1 October 2013 and 31 July 2022. Patients were divided into partial revision (n = 61) and full revision (n = 165) groups. The primary outcome was treatment success, defined as the absence of clinical symptoms and signs of infection at a minimum follow-up of 2 years.

RESULTS: The success rates were 77.0% for the partial revision group and 80.0% for the full revision group, with no significant difference (p = 0.629). Both groups showed comparable 10-year survival rates for overall success and infection-free status. Patients with partial revision had significantly shorter operative times (137.3 versus 169.1 min, p < 0.001). Age ≥ 65 years (odds ratios (OR): 2.433, p = 0.003), American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score ≥ 3 (OR: 1.778, p = 0.030), and chronic kidney disease (OR: 3.467, p = 0.053) were identified as independent risk factors for reinfection in the partial revision group.

CONCLUSIONS: Partial cementless single-stage revision may offer comparable infection control to full revision in selected hip PJI cases with well-fixed implants, while reducing operative time. Given the retrospective design, these findings should be interpreted with caution, and future prospective studies are needed to confirm long-term outcomes, assess implant survival, and evaluate functional recovery.

articles.title: Reproducibility of Two Novel Bone Defect Classification Systems.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To determine the reproducibility of 2 novel bone defect classification systems, the Tetsworth classification system and the universal long bone defect (ULBD) classification system.

METHODS: Two independent reproducibility studies were undertaken. A series of cases with bone defects was collected and sent to a panel of orthopaedic surgeons who were members of the OTA or Limb Lengthening and Reconstruction Society who routinely manage bone defects. The surgeons were provided with a measurement calibration scale for defect length assessment. Analysis of reproducibility was performed using a Fleiss multirater kappa model, where a Fleiss kappa of 0 indicated agreement no better than random chance, and 1 indicated perfect agreement. Surgeons also rated their confidence in their rating from 1 to 3, with 3 as "very confident."

RESULTS: For the Tetsworth classification, the Fleiss kappa was 0.264 for the overall classification system (fair agreement) (95% CI, 0.224-0.305). The kappa for the D1, D2, D3 part of the code related to defect completeness (incomplete, subcritical, or critical) was 0.557 (moderate agreement) (95% CI, 0.446-0.648). The kappa for the A, B, C part of the code related to defect shape was 0.402 (moderate agreement) (95% CI, 0.323-0.480). The mean confidence for all cases was 2.46 (range, 1.86-3). For the ULBD classification, the Fleiss kappa for the entire classification was 0.133 (slight agreement) (95% CI, 0.123-0.144). The kappa for the location and segment was 0.568 (moderate agreement) (95% CI, 0.526-0.610). The kappa for the morphology component was 0.124 (slight agreement) (95% CI, 0.114-0.135). The mean confidence for all cases was 2.0 (range, 1.0-3.0).

CONCLUSIONS: The bone defect classification system proposed by Tetsworth et al was reproducible by surgeons familiar with bone defects. The system can be considered for future research use. The ULBD classification system had low overall reproducibility.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Technical Tricks to Improve Iliosacral Screw Safety Using Three-dimensional Computed Tomography Imaging.
articles.abstract: This technical note describes a method used to facilitate iliosacral screw fixation with three-dimensional (3D) computed tomography (CT) imaging. Preoperative pelvis CT scans were used to generate 3D reconstructions, which were then manipulated into inlet and outlet orientations. The inlet position for S1 was achieved when the anterior cortex of the S1 body became superimposed on itself; the outlet position was when the S1 nerve root tunnel was viewed en face. On the fluoroscopic inlet view of S1, multiple cortical densities were often visible and could be difficult to distinguish as S1 versus other sacral segments. 3D CT helped distinguish the position and shape of the anterior cortical limit of S1 by referencing preoperative 3D CT inlet images that were reproduced intraoperatively on fluoroscopy using the appearance of the anterior pelvic ring and the relative obliquity of the obturator foramen. This technique was especially valuable in the setting of common posterior pelvic anatomic variations-including asymmetry, degenerative osteophytes, severe sacral slope, and dramatic cortical recesses of the upper sacral segment. These variations were often difficult to anticipate with conventional plain film or standard CT imaging alone, underscoring the potential clinical utility of this technique.

articles.title: Preoperative High-Sensitivity Troponin and Risk of In-Hospital Mortality and Cardiac Events After Hip Fracture Surgery.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether preoperative high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) elevation predicted in-hospital cardiac events and mortality after hip fracture surgery, and whether surgical delay modified this relationship.

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Single Level 1 trauma center in the United States.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adult patients who underwent hip fracture surgery between January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2024, and had a preoperative hs-cTn measurement as part of routine perioperative assessment were included.

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was a composite of in-hospital cardiac event or mortality. Secondary outcomes were in-hospital mortality and in-hospital cardiac events analyzed separately. Outcomes were compared across preoperative troponin categories defined as normal (<30 ng/L), elevated (30-100 ng/L), and significantly elevated (>100 ng/L), and across surgical delay categories defined as <24, 24-48, and >48 hours.

RESULTS: A total of 510 patients were included. The mean age was 76.3 ± 14.1 years, and 291 patients (57.1%) were female. Preoperative troponin was normal in 424 patients (83.1%), elevated in 58 patients (11.4%), and significantly elevated in 28 patients (5.5%). Thirty-five patients (6.9%) experienced the composite outcome. The composite outcome occurred in 19 of 424 patients (4.5%) with normal troponin, 6 of 58 patients (10.3%) with elevated troponin, and 10 of 28 patients (35.7%) with significantly elevated troponin ( P < 0.001). Mortality occurred in 8 of 424 patients (1.9%), 2 of 58 patients (3.4%), and 3 of 28 patients (10.7%), respectively ( P = 0.015). Cardiac events occurred in 13 of 424 patients (3.1%), 4 of 58 patients (6.9%), and 9 of 28 patients (32.1%), respectively ( P < 0.001). In adjusted models, elevated hs-cTn was associated with increased odds of the composite outcome (odds ratio 4.4, 95% confidence interval 1.1-17.9, P = 0.038), and significantly elevated troponin was associated with higher odds of the composite outcome (odds ratio 16.1, 95% confidence interval 3.6-72.4, P < 0.001). Higher American Society of Anesthesiologists class independently predicted the composite outcome and mortality, and longer length of stay was associated with cardiac events.

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative hs-cTn elevation was independently associated with in-hospital cardiac events and mortality after hip fracture surgery. Troponin levels greater than 100 ng/L identified patients at highest risk, independent of surgical delay.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Ballistic Forearm Fractures are Associated with Higher Neurovascular Injury, Nonunion, and Complications Compared With Blunt Forearm Injuries.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To characterize injury patterns, treatment differences, and clinical outcomes associated with ballistic and blunt forearm fractures.

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Single Level 1 tertiary trauma center, 2018-2023.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: The study included adults (≥18) who underwent operative fixation of diaphyseal radius and/or ulna fractures. Exclusion criteria were ipsilateral intraarticular or unstable elbow injuries, pathologic fractures, or fractures involving preexisting implants. Patients were stratified into 2 groups: ballistic and blunt injuries, which were further subclassified as blunt-closed or blunt-open.

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Primary outcomes included nerve deficit, complication rate, unplanned reoperation, nonunion, and postoperative infection.

RESULTS: The study included 395 patients with 398 forearm fractures: 81 ballistic fractures in 78 patients [32 years (18-69), 88.9% male], 213 blunt-closed fractures [41 years (18-82), 59.2% male], and 104 blunt-open fractures [46 years (19-92), 71.2% male]. Ballistic fractures had significantly higher rates of nerve deficits (48.2% vs. 6.3%, P < 0.001), complications (38.5% vs. 21.1%, P = 0.020), and unplanned reoperation (30.8% vs. 14.2%, P = 0.012) compared with blunt injuries. Infection rates were similar between ballistic and blunt groups (10.3% vs. 5.8%, P = 0.294). Nonunion differed only between ballistic and blunt-closed fractures (18.0% vs. 5.6%, P = 0.042), not blunt-open fractures (18.0% vs. 9.2%, P = 0.228). On multivariable analysis, injury group remained an independent predictor of nerve deficit ( P < 0.001), complication ( P = 0.008), and unplanned reoperation ( P = 0.015), with ballistic injuries demonstrating the highest rates.

CONCLUSIONS: Ballistic forearm fractures posed unique challenges compared with blunt injuries. They were associated with significantly higher rates of nerve deficit, unplanned reoperations, and overall complications, with higher nonunion observed when compared with blunt-closed injuries. These injuries warrant a high index of suspicion for nerve injury and close long-term follow-up to optimize patient outcomes and address the needs of a disproportionately affected, high-risk population.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: A Primer on Statistical Certainty and Its Distinction From Clinical Importance.

Nail-Plate Constructs Permit Early Weight Bearing and Improved Outcomes Compared With Single Device Constructs in the Treatment of Distal Femur Fractures at One-Year Follow-Up: A Retrospective Analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To investigate clinical, radiographic, and patient reported outcomes in patients undergoing surgical fixation for distal femur fractures with single device construct (lateral locked plate or intramedullary nail) or nail-plate combination.

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Single, academic, tertiary Level I trauma center.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: The inclusion criteria were patients with DFFs (OTA/AO 33) treated operatively with lateral locked plate, IM nail, or nail-plate combination between January 2011 and December 2023 with a minimum follow up of 1 year.

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Radiographic fracture healing, complication rates, weight-bearing status, length of stay, gait impairment, and patient-reported outcomes using the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System were investigated. Multivariable regression models were used to identify predictors of union, reoperation, discharge disposition, and postoperative complications.

RESULTS: A total of 191 patients were included, with 153 (131 lateral locked plate, 22 intramedullary nail) treated with a single device construct (mean age 72 years [range 22-95], 16% male) and 38 treated with nail-plate combination constructs (mean age 70 years [range 19-94], 16% male). At one-year postoperatively, nail-plate combination versus single device constructs were associated with significantly lower rates of nonunion (0% vs. 12%, P = 0.03), reoperation (10% vs. 26%, P = 0.05), and gait impairment (26% vs. 58%, P < 0.01). Patients in the nail-plate combination group versus the single device group were more likely to be weight bearing as tolerated at discharge (63% vs. 3%, P < 0.01) and more frequently discharged home (42% vs. 15%, P = 0.04).

CONCLUSIONS: Fixation with nail-plate combination constructs, compared with single device constructs, in DFFs seemed to support immediate weight bearing and was associated with improved short-term and midterm outcomes, including reduced rates of nonunion, reoperation, and functional impairment at 1 year. These advantages may be especially relevant for geriatric patients and those with complex or periprosthetic fracture patterns, or with preoperative risk factors for nonunion and functional decline.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Comparative Analysis of Nail Plate Combination Over Alternative Fixation Constructs in Low-Energy Distal Femur Fractures: Recovery of Ambulatory Status and Outcomes.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare ambulatory status, union, mortality, and operative complications in patients with distal femur fracture treated with the nail plate combination (NPC) and alternative fixation constructs.

DESIGN: Retrospective Cohort Study.

SETTING: Single Level 1, tertiary referral Academic center.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: This study included adults with a low-energy distal femur fracture (OTA/AO33A/C and Su 1-3) that received ORIF within 2018-2024. Exclusions were pathologic fractures, antegrade intramedullary devices, and baseline nonambulators (from ambulatory status evaluation only).

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was ambulatory status at postoperative intervals using Koval-Walking-Score. Secondary outcomes included radiographic union, mortality, and reoperation.

RESULTS: A total of 404 patients with a low-energy distal femur fracture were included, with 342 included for mobility analysis. Fixation constructs included 189 NPC (mean age 75.0 ± 10.2, 83.1% female), 118 lateral locking plate (LLP) (mean age 73.4 ± 10.2; 76.3% female), 79 retrograde intramedullary nail (rIMN) (mean age 73.7 ± 11.1, 74.7% female), and 18 dual plate combination (mean age 74.6 ± 10.9, 83.3% female) (age P = 0.567, sex P = 0.701). NPC was more frequently selected for Su 2 (56.2%) and Su 3 (65.9%) ( P = 0.001). NPC demonstrated lower average ambulatory impairment score over LLP: 3 weeks (-0.8; P = 0.002), 6 weeks (-1.1; P < 0.001), and both LLP and rIMN at 3 months (-0.9/-0.8; P = 0.049/0.013) and 6 months (-0.9/-0.8; P = 0.043/0.021). After Bonferroni correction to account for multiple testing, post hoc pairwise comparisons showed that NPC ambulation scores remained lower at 3 and 6 weeks (-0.8, P = 0.024; -1.1, P < 0.001). Six-month mortality was lower in NPC than rIMN (9% vs. 19%; P = 0.04). Dual plate combination showed higher infection (22.2%; P = 0.012), wound dehiscence (11.1%; P = 0.013), and drainage (5.6%; P < 0.001); although sample size limited analysis. Radiographic union was comparable (36.3% vs. 52.9% vs. 39.6% vs. 54.5%, P = 0.104).

CONCLUSIONS: In this study, NPC was associated with superior ambulatory recovery rates to preinjury status over single-implant constructs and improved mortality rates over rIMN. Thus, NPC represented a reliable construct for early ambulation and recovery in these injuries.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Single Antibiotic Use With Ceftriaxone for Prophylaxis of All Open Fractures.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare outcomes for open fractures treated with a prophylactic antibiotic protocol using ceftriaxone (CTX) for all open fractures, referred to as group "CTX," versus a previous protocol using cefazolin for Gustilo I/II fractures and cefazolin plus gentamicin or CTX monotherapy for Gustilo type III fractures only, referred to as group "Classic."

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study.

SETTING: Single level I trauma center.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: This study included adult patients undergoing surgery for an open fracture from December 2016 to December 2022 with a minimum follow-up of 3 months.

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome of deep infection and secondary outcomes of superficial infection rates, nonunion rate, and time to antibiotic administration were compared between overall groups and subgroups based on Gustilo type.

RESULTS: A total of 521 patients were included. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, with no differences in age (CTX 41.1 ± 19.7 vs. classic 39.5 ± 19.3), sex (68.5% vs. 72.0% male), or comorbidities ( P > 0.05). There were no differences in deep infection (7.8% vs. 12.7%, P = 0.095), superficial infection (7.0% vs. 4.7%, P = 0.427), or nonunion (10.3% vs. 7.9%, P = 0.500) between CTX and Classic groups for all Gustilo types. Similarly for only type I/II fractures, rates of deep infection (3.5% vs. 8.9%, P = 0.145), superficial infection (2.9% vs. 3.6%, P = 0.683), and nonunion (3.6% vs. 0.0%, P = 0.340) did not differ. Noninferiority of CTX for deep infection was demonstrated for all Gustilo types (intergroup difference -0.048, P = 0.027) and type I/II fractures (-0.054, P = 0.035). The CTX protocol was associated with shorter time to antibiotic administration (63.9 ± 116.9 vs. 114.1 ± 199.0 minutes, P = 0.002).

CONCLUSIONS: The use of CTX for prophylaxis of all open fractures, regardless of Gustilo type, was associated with noninferior outcomes in deep infection as well as shorter time to antibiotic administration, compared with a regimen where type I/II fractures received cefazolin. No significant differences in rates of superficial infection or nonunion were noted after transition to CTX protocol. The study was notably underpowered to detect a difference in the primary outcome of deep infection. Prophylaxis of all open fractures with CTX may be a safe and effective method of standardizing and expediting care for orthopaedic trauma patients.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Temporal Effects on Intraoperative Bacterial Contamination of Surgical Gloves in Noninfection Orthopaedic Trauma Cases.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Surgical site infections (SSIs) are among the most serious complications in orthopaedic trauma surgery, contributing to patient morbidity, mortality, and substantial financial costs. With direct inoculation from intraoperative bacterial contamination being a large contributor to these infections, the temporal dynamics of intraoperative bacterial colonization on surgical gloves in orthopaedic trauma cases was investigated.

METHODS: Surgical glove bacterial cultures were taken by firmly pressing the operating room staff member's gloved fingertips onto a sheep's blood agar plate. Cases, without known preexisting infection, were chosen from a single level 1 trauma center at random between 2023 and 2025. Samples were obtained at 2 intraoperative time points: (1) immediately after draping and (2) after implant placement but before final irrigation. These samples were compared with negative controls of freshly donned, but unused sterile gloves. Glove imprints were then incubated for 2 weeks, and bacterial isolates were identified using MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry.

RESULTS: Of 276 total gloves sampled, 70 (25.4% 70/138) demonstrated bacterial growth, compared with 0 controls (0%, 0/138 P < 0.001). Contamination was detected in 18.8% of gloves after draping and 31.9% after implant placement. Pelvic procedures had the highest contamination rate by surgical location (58.3%, P < 0.05 vs. 20.2% upper extremities and 25.5% lower extremities). Compared with gloves without bacterial growth, mean glove wear duration was longer for contaminated gloves (86.5 vs. 77.4 minutes, P = 0.043), with significantly lower rates observed at ≤75 minutes of wear ( P = 0.049). The most common isolate was Staphylococcus epidermidis (20.5%), which was more commonly grown at the second collection time point.

CONCLUSIONS: Intraoperative surgical gloves demonstrated high rates of bacterial contamination, particularly with longer procedure times. Routine glove changes after draping, after final implant placement, and after >75 minutes of operating time may be a simple, low-cost strategy to reduce potential SSI risk.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Prognostic Level IV. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Functional Outcomes After Bipolar Hip Hemiarthroplasty by Using the Direct Anterior Approach Versus Posterior and Direct Lateral Approaches: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To compare functional recovery and length of hospital stay in patients undergoing bipolar hip hemiarthroplasty (BHH) for displaced femoral neck fractures using the direct anterior approach (DAA) versus the posterior approach (PA) and direct lateral approach (DLA).

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study using a prospectively maintained hip fracture registry.

SETTING: Single tertiary care institution in Singapore.

PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Patients aged 60 years and older who underwent BHH for displaced femoral neck fractures (OTA/AO 31-B) between 2020 and 2023 were identified from the institutional hip fracture registry.

OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: Functional outcomes were assessed using the Modified Barthel Index (MBI; higher scores indicate better independence) and Parker Mobility Score (higher scores indicate better mobility) at discharge, 6 and 12 months. Mobility status, length of stay, postoperative complications, reoperation, and 1-year mortality were evaluated. Outcomes were compared between DAA and PA after propensity score matching, with an exploratory comparison with the DLA.

RESULTS: A total of 504 patients were identified; 400 PA, 79 DAA, and 25 DLA. After matching, 67 DAA cases and 134 PA cases were analyzed. Age and sex distribution were similar between DAA and PA groups (80.7 ± 6.3 vs. 81.1 ± 6.5 years, P = 0.655; female: 79.1% vs. 75.4%, P = 0.556). The DAA group demonstrated a smaller decline in MBI from premorbid baseline to discharge as compared with the PA group [DAA: -49.85 ± 17.88 vs. PA: -55.47 ± 18.90, 95% confidence interval (CI): 0.11-11.13, P = 0.045]. No significant differences were observed between the DAA and PA groups in changes from premorbid to 12-month MBI (DAA: -23.97 ± 27.46 vs. PA: -18.52 ± 26.38, 95% CI: -13.67 to 2.78, P = 0.193) or from premorbid to 12-month Parker Mobility Score (DAA: -2.72 ± 2.90 vs. PA: -2.18 ± 2.46, 95% CI: -1.37 to 0.29, P = 0.198). Length of stay (DAA: 9.88 ± 5.08 vs. PA: 10.20 ± 5.20 days; P = 0.684) and 1-year mortality (DAA: 3.0% vs. PA: 8.2%; P = 0.156) were comparable between DAA and PA groups.

CONCLUSIONS: DAA for BHH was associated with better early functional recovery at hospital discharge than PA. However, this advantage did not persist at 12 months, with no significant differences in functional outcomes, length of hospital stay, or 1-year mortality between DAA and PA groups.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Patient-Reported Outcomes after Distal Radius Fractures Differ Across Geographic and Cultural Populations: A Global Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To assess patient reported outcome (PRO) heterogeneity across different cultural and geographical regions through a systematic review and meta-analysis of PROs after volar plate fixation of distal radius fractures.

DATA SOURCES: PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials were queried for randomized controlled trials from 2010 to 2023 reporting Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (DASH), QuickDASH, Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE), or Visual Analog Scale (VAS) PROs.

STUDY SELECTION: Randomized controlled trials with treatment arms consisting of open reduction and internal fixation using a volar locking plate for adult distal radius fracture (OTA/AO 23) and reported DASH, QuickDASH, PRWE, or VAS PROs were included. Studies not published in English or that provided insufficient extraction data were excluded.

DATA EXTRACTION: Studies were characterized by country of origin, continent of origin, and cultural region of origin. Extracted data included PRO outcomes, patient demographics, and follow-up ranges.

DATA SYNTHESIS: Random-effects meta-analysis was performed with restricted maximum likelihood method, and subgroup analyses were performed to determine differences in pooled PROs across geographical and cultural regions.

RESULTS: A total of 52 treatment arms met inclusion criteria for DASH analysis, 33 for PRWE, and 23 for VAS. Significant mean DASH score heterogeneity existed across all studies ( P < 0.01). Nine cultural regions were represented in the DASH analysis and demonstrated significantly different pooled mean PRO scores ( P < 0.01). Significant mean PRWE score heterogeneity existed across all studies ( P < 0.01). Seven cultural regions were represented in the PRWE analysis and demonstrated significantly different pooled mean PRO scores ( P < 0.01). Significant mean VAS score heterogeneity existed across all studies ( P < 0.01). Eight cultural regions were represented in the VAS analysis and demonstrated significantly different pooled mean PRO scores ( P < 0.01).

CONCLUSIONS: PROs after distal radius volar plate fixation demonstrated meaningful variation across cultural and geographic contexts. Outcomes from one cultural region may not be globally generalizable.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic Level II. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

articles.title: Novel bicolumnar fixation with primary cup implantation for pelvic discontinuity in revision hip arthroplasty: a comparative clinical study.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pelvic discontinuity is a rare but challenging condition in revision hip arthroplasty. Traditional cage-based reconstruction techniques often rely solely on mechanical fixation and may be associated with implant migration, loosening, and mechanical failure. Alternative strategies aimed at restoring pelvic continuity and achieving biological fixation may improve construct stability and clinical outcomes.

METHODS: This retrospective study included 19 patients with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity who underwent revision total hip arthroplasty between 2014 and 2024. Patients were divided into three groups according to the reconstruction technique used: Group 1 (n = 8) underwent anti-protrusio cage reconstruction alone, Group 2 (n = 6) received additional anterior quadrilateral surface plating prior to cage implantation, and Group 3 (n = 5) underwent restoration of pelvic continuity through anterior and posterior column fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup. Clinical and radiological outcomes were assessed with a minimum follow-up of 2 years, including complications, loosening, reoperation, and reoperation-free survival.

RESULTS: Nineteen patients (mean age 71.2 years) with intraoperatively confirmed pelvic discontinuity were included. Aseptic loosening rates differed significantly among the three groups (P = 0.039), occurring in 50% of patients in Group 1 and in none of the patients in Groups 2 or 3. Reoperation rates were higher in Group 1 (75%) than in Group 2 (16.7%) and Group 3 (20%), although this difference did not reach statistical significance (P = 0.074). Kaplan-Meier analysis demonstrated a trend toward lower reoperation-free survival in Group 1; however, differences among the groups were not statistically significant (log-rank P = 0.237).

CONCLUSION: Reconstruction strategies involving restoration of pelvic continuity through column stabilization may provide improved mechanical stability and lower complication rates compared with conventional cage-only techniques in the management of pelvic discontinuity. In selected patients, bicolumnar fixation followed by implantation of a porous-coated primary acetabular cup may offer the additional advantage of biological fixation. Larger prospective studies are needed to validate these findings.

articles.title: Arthroplasty centers logistically separated from general orthopedic departments were associated with a more successful implementation of a standardized day-case setup : A Danish cohort study of 6718 procedures from a fast-track multi-center collaboration.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Day-case hip and knee arthroplasty can reduce bed occupancy and improve cost-effectiveness, which is crucial for addressing the increasing demand among hip and knee osteoarthritis patients. This study investigated how different arthroplasty center setups were associated with the implementation and day-of-surgery (DOS) discharge rates of a standardized day-case setup.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We included unilateral primary hip and knee arthroplasty patients from seven fast-track arthroplasty centers, all implementing a standardized day-case setup in September 2022 with identical eligibility and discharge criteria. Centers were categorized as: Satellite Arthroplasty Centers (SACs): Only primary arthroplasties, separate logistics. Elective Arthroplasty Centers (EACs): Complex primaries, revisions, separate logistics. Arthroplasty Unit Orthopedic Departments (AUOs): Primary and revision procedures, integrated into a general orthopedic department. We compared DOS discharge rates from September 2022 to September 2023 with a baseline period (July 2019-December 2019) using crude percentages. We compared the DOS discharge rate for day-case-eligible patients in study period between the center types using mixed effects models.

RESULTS: We included 6718 patients (1357 SAC, 4309 EAC, 1052 AUO) during the study period and 3974 in the baseline period. DOS discharge rates increased post-implementation across all centers (SAC: 3.9% to 30%, EAC: 5.5% to 23%, AUO: 7.4% to 14%). Compared with AUOs (36%), successful DOS discharge among eligible patients was more likely in SACs (54%; adjusted OR 3.0, 95% CI 1.3-7.1; adjusted risk difference 25 percentage points, 95% CI 5.9-44) and EACs (60%; adjusted OR 3.8, 95% CI 1.7-8.5; adjusted risk difference 31 percentage points, 95% CI 13.8-48).

CONCLUSIONS: Arthroplasty centers with logistics separate from the general orthopedic department, SACs and EACs, were associated with higher rates of successful DOS discharge among eligible patients during implementation of a standardized day-case pathway, despite integrated arthroplasty units, AUOs, having higher day-case surgery use before implementation.

articles.title: Preoperative coronal tibiofemoral subluxation does not affect 2-year outcomes after mobile-bearing medial unicompartmental knee arthroplasty for anteromedial osteoarthritis.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Coronal tibiofemoral subluxation (CTFS) is frequently observed in patients with medial knee osteoarthritis; however, its clinical relevance and the acceptable degree of CTFS when considering unicompartmental knee arthroplasty (UKA) remain unclear. This study aimed to determine whether preoperative CTFS influences short-term postoperative clinical outcomes in patients with anteromedial osteoarthritis (AMOA) undergoing medial UKA.

METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, 457 consecutive knees with AMOA who underwent mobile-bearing UKA performed at a single center between August 2016 and May 2023 were analyzed. CTFS, defined as medial translation of the femur relative to the tibia, was measured on preoperative weight-bearing anteroposterior radiographs and expressed as the percentage of tibial plateau width. Patients were categorized into mild (0-5%), moderate (≥ 5% to < 10%), and severe (≥ 10%) CTFS groups. Clinical outcomes were evaluated using the Oxford Knee Score (OKS) preoperatively and at 3 months, 1 and 2 years postoperatively. Pairwise comparisons of changes in OKS were performed using a general linear model with Bonferroni-adjusted post hoc tests, and adjusted mean differences were calculated controlling for age, sex, body mass index, and preoperative OKS.

RESULTS: At 2 years, mean OKS improvements were 16.6 ± 8.9, 14.8 ± 8.3, and 16.0 ± 9.3 in the mild, moderate, and severe CTFS groups, respectively. Adjusted mean differences between groups were small, with confidence intervals including zero. The severe CTFS group demonstrated greater joint line convergence angle than the mild and moderate groups (both p < 0.001). Mean bearing thickness did not differ among groups (p = 0.428).

CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative CTFS was not associated with worse outcomes in mobile-bearing UKA for AMOA with correctable deformity. Within the setting of correctable deformity and appropriate patient selection, preoperative CTFS was not associated with inferior 2-year outcomes. Longer-term survivorship and radiographic progression analyses are warranted.

articles.title: Radial head arthroplasty restores axial construct stiffness in a Monteggia-like injury model: a biomechanical study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Monteggia-like lesions are rare but complex elbow injuries involving fractures of both the proximal ulna and the radial head. While the influence of ulnar alignment and soft tissue integrity on radial head stability has been extensively studied, the effect of radial head integrity on the stability of ulnar fixation remains poorly understood. Given the high rates of nonunion and revision surgery after proximal ulna fractures, improved understanding of forearm biomechanics in these combined injuries is highly clinically relevant as it influences the surgical strategy in primary care of these injuries. Accordingly, this study aimed to evaluate the biomechanical impact of radial head resection and radial head arthroplasty on forearm stiffness in a simulated Monteggia-like injury model. We hypothesized that radial head resection would reduce construct stiffness compared with both the native state and radial head arthroplasty, and that arthroplasty would partially restore stiffness toward native levels MATERIALS AND METHODS: Eight fresh-frozen human cadaveric elbow specimens were biomechanically tested under axial loading. After baseline testing in the native state, a standardized segmental comminution model was created and stabilized using locking plate osteosynthesis. Sequential testing was then performed after radial head resection and after implantation of a modular radial head prosthesis. Specimens were loaded cyclically up to 450 N for 1,000 cycles with the elbow positioned at 30° of flexion. Construct stiffness was calculated and compared between testing conditions.

RESULTS: Mean construct stiffness in the native state was 49.3 ± 4.29 N/mm and decreased significantly after creation and fixation of the ulnar defect (36.05 ± 6.71 N/mm). Radial head resection resulted in a further significant reduction in stiffness (25.83 ± 6.65 N/mm). Following radial head arthroplasty, stiffness increased to 33.8 ± 7.89 N/mm, representing a significant improvement compared with the resection state (p ≤ 0.0026). No significant difference was observed between stiffness after prosthesis implantation and the condition with intact radial head and stabilized ulna.

CONCLUSION: Radial head integrity significantly contributes to forearm stiffness in Monteggia-like lesions. Radial head arthroplasty partially restores biomechanical stability after resection and may alter load distribution in a manner that could be relevant for fixation durability. These findings support the need to address the radial column to optimize stability in complex elbow injuries.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Biomechanical study.

articles.title: Correction: Single double-loaded anchor repair of isolated Lafosse III subscapularis tears in patients not involved in physically demanding activities provides satisfactory functional and radiologic outcomes at minimum 5-year follow-up.
Comparison of surgically treated floating elbow injuries and supracondylar humeral fractures in children.
articles.abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Floating elbow is a rare injury type in pediatric fractures. This study compared the differences in injury mechanisms, treatment modalities, complications and prognosis between floating elbow injury and supracondylar humerus fractures (SHF) in children in a surgically treated cohort.

METHODS: The retrospective analysis included patients with floating elbow and SHF treated at our hospital between May 2016 and May 2023. Sex, age, body mass index (BMI), mechanism of injury, affected limb, fracture displacement, presence of neurovascularinjury, type of injury, Gartland classification, and acute compartment syndrome (ACS) were analyzed. Elbow function was evaluated using the Mayo Elbow Performance Score (MEPS). ACS was defined by clinical criteria including pain, paresthesia, and/or compartment pressure > 30 mmHg.

RESULTS: A total of 113 children were enrolled, including 27 in the floating elbow group (22 males, 5 females, median age 8 years [IQR 6-11 years]), and 86 in the SHF group (58 males, 28 females, median age 8 years [IQR 5-10 years]). Mechanism of injury (p = 0.001), fracture type (p = 0.003), and preoperative nerve injury (p = 0.001) differed significantly between the two groups. ACS incidence differed significantly between open and closed fractures in the floating elbow group (p = 0.028); however, this finding is based on a small number of events.

CONCLUSION: In this surgically treated cohort, we did not detect statistically significant differences in elbow function outcomes between children with floating elbow and those with isolated SHF. Open fractures were associated with a higher incidence of ACS in the floating elbow group compared with closed fractures, although the number of events was small (p = 0.028). Larger studies are needed to confirm equivalence or identify clinically meaningful differences.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: III.

articles.title: Platelet-rich plasma for knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of structural outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: To assess the impact of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) on imaging-based structural outcomes in patients with knee osteoarthritis (OA).

METHODS: PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) published up to May 2026 evaluating imaging-based structural effects of PRP in knee OA. Risk ratio (RR) was used to evaluate binary outcomes and standardized mean differences (SMDs) or mean differences (MDs) for continuous endpoints, with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).

RESULTS: A total of 12 RCTs involving 1,200 patients were included. PRP was associated with greater improvement in patellofemoral cartilage thickness/volume compared with control treatments (SMD 0.94; 95% CI, 0.53 to 1.34), whereas no significant differences were observed for medial tibial cartilage thickness/volume or cartilage defect progression. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based structural scores showed no between-group differences in Whole-Organ Magnetic Resonance Imaging Score (WORMS) osteophytes or subchondral cysts, although PRP demonstrated a significant reduction in bone marrow edema (SMD - 0.40; 95% CI, - 0.71 to - 0.09). Synovitis did not differ overall between groups (SMD - 0.22; 95% CI, - 0.43 to 0.00).

CONCLUSION: In this systematic review and meta-analysis, PRP demonstrated limited and inconsistent effects on imaging-based structural outcomes in knee OA, and did not confer significant and consistent benefits in medial tibial cartilage measurements, cartilage defect progression, synovitis, or most WORMS domains. The favorable findings observed for patellofemoral cartilage and bone marrow edema should be interpreted with caution. Thus, the findings do not provide clear evidence supporting PRP as a structural disease-modifying treatment, and additional high-quality RCTs using standardized imaging endpoints are warranted.

articles.title: First-in-human prospective pilot study of a bipolar dual-center total wrist arthroplasty: early mechanical stability and clinical outcomes.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Total wrist arthroplasty (TWA) is limited by implant loosening, instability, and non-physiological load transfer, partly because most contemporary implants rely on a single center of rotation and do not preserve native wrist kinematics. This first-in-human pilot study evaluated the feasibility, early mechanical stability, and clinical outcomes of a novel bipolar dual-center TWA system designed to preserve radiocarpal and midcarpal motion.

METHODS: This prospective single-center pilot case series included five consecutive patients with end-stage wrist arthritis treated with a bipolar dual-center TWA implant using cement fixation, as per the device's intended use. The outcome measures included pain assessed using the pain subscale of the Patient-Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) questionnaire (normalized to a 0-10 scale), total PRWE score, DASH score, range of motion, grip strength, radiographic implant stability, complications, and reoperation. Clinical outcomes were assessed at the most recent follow-up visit.

RESULTS: The mean follow-up was 19.2 months (range, 12-24 months), with 24-month data available for three patients. Implant survivorship was 100%, with no loosening, migration, dislocation, or implant revision observed on radiographs. One patient experienced a traumatic postoperative fall without loss of implant fixation. The mean PRWE-derived pain score improved from 9.0 to 3.0, and the mean PRWE total improved from 84.6 to 23.2 at the final follow-up. The mean DASH score improved from 79.0 to 29.5, with substantial inter-patient variability (final range, 0-91.7). All five patients met the predefined responder criterion of ΔPRWE ≥ 20 combined with radiographic stability. Three patients with positive preoperative signs of carpal tunnel syndrome subsequently underwent carpal tunnel release 4-8 months postoperatively, with symptomatic improvement in all patients. One intraoperative carpal fracture was managed without component revision surgery. The mean wrist flexion improved from 13° to 37°, and extension improved from 11° to 32°.

CONCLUSIONS: This first-in-human pilot study demonstrated the technical feasibility and early mechanical stability of the bipolar dual-center TWA concept. All patients met the predefined wrist-specific responder criteria with stable mechanical implant fixation. These findings support further investigation of the dual-center concept in larger studies with longer follow-up periods.

articles.title: The reliability and validity of the 30-Second Fast-Paced Walk Test in patients with total knee arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Walking speed is a significant measure of functional ability and recovery after total knee arthroplasty (TKA). The 30-Second Fast-Paced Walk Test (30SFW) is a simple, low-cost, and easy-to-administer assessment method that evaluates short-distance walking ability.

OBJECTIVE: To investigate the reliability and validity of the 30SFW test in patients with TKA.

METHODS: This study was designed as a repeated-measures study conducted by one assessor. 38 patients with TKA who had undergone primary TKA at least 6 months earlier (mean age 70.11 ± 10.19 years) were included in the study. The 30SFW, the Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) Knee Score, and Short Form (SF)-12 Quality of Life Questionnaire were administered to the patients. The 30SFW was administered twice at a single center on the same day, with an hour-long rest interval between sessions.

RESULTS: The test-retest reliability of the 30SFW was excellent. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC [2, 1]), minimal detectable change (MDC95), and standard error of the measurement (SEM) values were 0.98, 2.91, and 1.05, respectively, at the 95% confidence level. The Pearson correlation coefficient of the 30SFW with the physical component of the SF-12 was 0.45 (p = 0.005).

CONCLUSION: The 30SFW has excellent test-retest reliability and moderate concurrent validity in assessing walking ability in patients with TKA. The MDC95 was 2.91 m, indicating the minimum change required to exceed measurement error under similar testing conditions. Further studies are needed to determine the clinically important change and responsiveness of the 30SFW in this population.

articles.title: Net present value analysis of total salary compensation in hand surgery: academic versus non-academic careers.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Studies comparing salary compensation of hand surgeons in different practice settings have been limited. This study compared projected lifetime salary compensation between academic and non-academic hand surgeons.

METHODS: Compensation data were sourced from the 2025 Medical Group Management Association (MGMA) and American Medical Group Association (AMGA) salary benchmarks. Net present values of theoretical career paths in hand surgery were calculated assuming a 32-year career and a 3% discount rate. Sensitivity analyses were performed with variable discount rates and career lengths. Monte Carlo simulations were performed.

RESULTS: Academic practice demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice across career trajectories, sensitivity analyses, and Monte Carlo simulations using MGMA data with minimal differences using AMGA data. With MGMA, academic practice ($12.6 million) resulted in 19.7% lower lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice ($15.7 million). With AMGA, academic practice ($15.0 million) resulted in 2.7% higher lifetime salary compensation than non-academic practice ($14.6 million). Monte Carlo simulations demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation for academic practice with MGMA ($12.9 million versus $16.0 million, 19.4% difference, P < 0.001) but comparable compensation with AMGA data ($15.1 million versus $15.0 million, 0.7% difference, P = 0.182).

CONCLUSION: Hand surgeons in academic practice demonstrated lower lifetime salary compensation than their non-academic counterparts using MGMA data and similar compensation using AMGA data. While compensation alone does not fully capture the complexity of career decision making, this study may be useful to future hand surgeons and service line leaders.

articles.title: Complicated labral injuries in female patients with developmental dysplasia of the hip are associated with localized stress concentration in the superior acetabulum.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) alters joint mechanics and increases the risk of labral injury, compromising hip stability and leading to abnormal stress distribution and cartilage degeneration. However, the relationship between labral injury severity and joint loading stress in DDH remains unclear. This study investigated the effect of labral injury severity on stress distribution in DDH patients using computed tomography osteoabsorptometry (CT-OAM) and finite element analysis.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: We analyzed 54 hips from 45 female patients undergoing joint-preserving surgery for DDH. Labral injuries were classified as simple or complicated on radial MRI. Subchondral bone density distribution was evaluated with CT-OAM, while finite element analysis of pelvic and femoral bones with cartilage was performed under a single-leg stance to assess contact pressure and area. Statistical analyses examined associations between labral injury severity and stress distribution.

RESULTS: Superior injuries showed significantly increased high-density area (HDA) in the superior acetabulum, indicating localized stress concentration (simple injury vs. complicated injury, 64.4% vs. 80.3%, p < 0.001). However, finite element analysis revealed no significant differences in contact pressure or area (simple vs. complicated, 5.3 N/mm² vs. 6.2 N/mm², p = 0.538), which we interpret as showing that bony morphology alone could not explain the observed stress patterns. Instead, the discrepancy highlights the role of labral failure reflected in CT-derived subchondral bone density.

CONCLUSION: Complicated labral injuries, especially superiorly, were associated with localized stress accumulation in DDH.

articles.title: Postoperative alignment and patients reported outcome measures improvement after high tibial osteotomy: a significant interaction with osteoarthritis severity.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Optimal postoperative alignment in high tibial osteotomy (HTO) remains controversial due to inconsistent target definitions and limited evidence supporting osteoarthritis (OA) severity-based strategies. This study evaluated clinical outcomes across postoperative weight-bearing line (WBL) categories stratified by OA severity, hypothesizing that overcorrection would be detrimental in early OA but not in advanced OA.

METHODS: This retrospective single-center study included 181 knees that underwent open-wedge or closed-wedge HTO between 2017 and 2023 with a minimum 2-year follow-up. Knees were classified as early OA (Kellgren-Lawrence [KL] ≤ 2) or advanced OA (KL ≥ 3). The corrective angle was defined as the planned angular change required to shift the mechanical axis to the target postoperative alignment, determined by aiming for a postoperative %WBL of 62.5% on double-limb standing full-length radiographs. Overcorrection was defined as %WBL ≥ 70%. Clinical and radiographic outcomes were assessed at baseline and final follow-up. Multivariable regression models identified factors associated with changes (Δ) in Forgotten Joint Score-12 (FJS-12) and Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), and logistic regression evaluated achievement of minimum clinically important difference (MCID) and patient acceptable symptom state (PASS). Each knee was treated as an independent observational unit.

RESULTS: Early OA (n = 112) and advanced OA (n = 69) showed comparable baseline characteristics. In early OA, postoperative alignment was significantly associated with ΔFJS‑12 and ΔKOOS Sports. Compared with optimal alignment, overcorrection was associated with smaller improvement in ΔFJS‑12 (β = -10.49, 95% CI - 20.46 to - 0.53) and ΔKOOS Sports, whereas undercorrection did not demonstrate a statistically significant association with postoperative improvement. Overcorrection also reduced the likelihood of achieving MCID and PASS in early OA. In advanced OA, postoperative alignment was not associated with PROM improvements or MCID/PASS achievement.

CONCLUSIONS: Overcorrection was associated with significantly poorer improvement in FJS-12 and KOOS Sports in early OA, whereas postoperative alignment was not associated with differences in PROM improvements in advanced OA.

LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: IV.

articles.title: Analysis of serological markers and synovial fluid cytology in aseptic revision total knee arthroplasty.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND AIM: Recent studies examining synovial fluid analysis to differentiate causes for aseptic revision total knee arthroplasty (rTKA) were limited to aseptic loosening and instability. This study aims to establish specific serological and synovial profiles for various rTKA etiologies.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed patients who underwent aseptic rTKA at a single academic institution between 2012 and 2023. Inclusion required complete serum inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP)) and synovial fluid differentials within three months pre-operatively. Periprosthetic joint infections were strictly excluded utilizing the 2018 International Consensus Meeting criteria. In total, 156 patients were included and stratified into five aseptic etiologies: aseptic loosening (50.6%), instability (28.2%), arthrofibrosis (16.7%), liner wear (2.6%), and component malposition (1.9%). Serological markers were evaluated utilizing a multivariate general linear model adjusting for patient demographics, while synovial markers were assessed via Welch's Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Games-Howell post-hoc testing.

RESULTS: Multivariate analysis demonstrated that the underlying rTKA indication was not a significant independent predictor of elevated ESR (P = 0.661) or CRP (P = 0.947). Welch's ANOVA revealed significant differences in the percentage of synovial monocytes (P < 0.001) and lymphocytes (P = 0.010), alongside the polymorphonuclear cells/monocyte (P = 0.030) and lymphocyte/monocyte (P = 0.005) ratios. Games-Howell post-hoc testing demonstrated the tibial liner wear group exhibited significantly higher monocyte percentages, paired with lower lymphocyte percentages and cellular ratios, compared to other aseptic etiologies.

CONCLUSIONS: This study revealed that routine systemic inflammatory markers and standard synovial fluid cell counts do not significantly vary among the common etiologies of aseptic rTKA. Nonetheless, tibial polyethylene liner wear appears to elicit an exploratory, monocyte-predominant and lymphocyte-depleted local macrophage response that is absent in other mechanisms of aseptic failure. Further research with larger cohorts is warranted to validate this association and explore its potential as a diagnostic tool.

articles.title: Clinical outcomes and feasibility of a fast-track protocol after total ankle replacement: a prospective study.
articles.abstract:
PURPOSE: Postoperative recovery after total ankle replacement remains challenging, and evidence supporting the use of fast-track protocols in this setting is limited. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the short-term clinical outcomes and safety of a fast-track protocol following total ankle replacement.

METHODS: A prospective observational study was conducted on consecutive adult patients undergoing primary total ankle replacement through an anterior approach between January 2023 and June 2024. All procedures were performed by a single experienced surgeon using the same implant. The fast-track protocol included early postoperative mobilization, multimodal pain management, bleeding control, and structured physiotherapy with standardized discharge criteria. Ankle function was assessed using the American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society's (AOFAS) Ankle Hindfoot Scale preoperatively and at hospital discharge. Secondary outcomes included time to active ankle mobilization, time to assisted ambulation with crutches, length of hospital stay, and wound healing evaluated using the ASEPSIS wound score.

RESULTS: Twenty-two patients were included. Median AOFAS Ankle Hindfoot Scale scores improved significantly from 29.0 preoperatively to 68.0 at discharge. Active ankle mobilization was achieved after a median of two days, assisted ambulation after three days, and the median hospital stay was five days. Wound healing outcomes were favourable, with low ASEPSIS scores and only one minor wound complication managed conservatively. No major wound complications, infections, or prosthesis-related adverse events were observed.

CONCLUSION: In this prospective single-arm study, a fast-track protocol following total ankle replacement was feasible and was associated with early functional recovery and favourable short-term safety outcomes. These findings should be interpreted as preliminary and descriptive, given the absence of a control group. Larger comparative studies with longer follow-up are needed to determine its effectiveness relative to conventional postoperative care.

articles.title: Patient-specific management in high-risk revision total hip arthroplasty: mid-term outcomes of a next-generation constrained acetabular liner.
articles.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Managing recurrent instability in revision total hip arthroplasty (rTHA) requires a personalized approach, as traditional constrained liners often yield suboptimal results due to locking-mechanism failure and limited impingement-free range of motion. This study aimed to evaluate the mid-term clinical outcomes of a novel constrained acetabular liner (CAL) when utilized as a patient-specific solution for a high-risk cohort undergoing complex rTHA. By tailoring the constraint to individual biomechanical deficits, this next-generation device seeks to mitigate historic failure modes.

METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 32 patients who underwent 37 rTHA procedures with a next-generation CAL at a single urban academic center between March 2017 and October 2023. Average follow-up was 4.7 years (range, 0.3 to 9.7 years). The most common indication for rTHA was instability (70.3%), followed by infection (16.2%), aseptic loosening (10.8%), and polyethylene wear (2.7%). Just over one third of patients (37.5%) had undergone a prior revision. Preoperative constructs included fixed-bearing (37.8%), dual-mobility (32.4%), CAL (24.3%), static spacer (2.7%), and hemiarthroplasty (2.7%).

RESULTS: In most procedures (70.3%), the CAL was implanted into a pre-existing acetabular cup, whereas 29.7% involved both cup and liner revision. Following rTHA, no cases of implant wear, breakage, acetabular cup aseptic loosening, or periprosthetic fracture were observed. Six patients (18.8%) underwent a total of sixteen subsequent reoperations after CAL implantation-10 for instability and 6 for infection. Among instability-related reoperations, 4 involved revision to a new next-generation CAL. Survivorship free from all-cause reoperation was 83.8% at one year and 72.6% at latest follow-up.

CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates favorable mid-term clinical outcomes and reoperation-free survivorship following complex revision THA using a novel constrained acetabular liner system. For patient cohorts suffering from severe recurrent dislocation, this next-generation CAL provides an effective, tailored tool in the surgical armamentarium by adapting to unique patient anatomy and soft-tissue compromises. Further research with larger sample sizes and extended follow-up is needed to assess long-term durability.

articles.title: Diagnostic accuracy of standard practice wrist MRI for scapholunate ligament injuries: a retrospective arthroscopic correlation study.
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The scapholunate ligament is the most injured intercarpal ligament. Untreated tears can lead to carpal instability and subsequent radiocarpal and midcarpal osteoarthritis. While wrist arthroscopy remains the gold standard, the diagnostic performance of standard practice preoperative MRI in clinical practice warrants further investigation.

METHODS: We retrospectively analysed patients who underwent preoperative wrist MRI followed by wrist arthroscopy between 2013 and 2021.
